blocks.text: The opening presents this work both as a revelation of Jesus Christ and as prophecy. It introduces what follows as a message meant to be read, heard, and kept, framing the visions as words addressed to servants rather than as detached speculation.

This book is addressed to seven assemblies in Roman Asia, identified by city. The vision is therefore introduced within a direct address to particular communities, even as its imagery reaches beyond the opening greeting.

Revelation combines features of apocalypse, prophecy, and circular letter. John identifies himself simply as John, without explicitly claiming apostolic identity, and says he was on Patmos because of God’s word and Jesus’s testimony; the text does not state that this was a legal sentence. These limits matter when readers try to supply details the chapter itself does not give.

Revelation reuses Danielic imagery—including humanlike-figure, beast, horn, time, saint, book, and judgment imagery—in a new literary setting. This makes the chapter’s striking visions part of a larger pattern of scriptural imagery rather than a set of isolated pictures.

As Revelation continues, it repeatedly reworks Israel’s Scriptures, especially Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Exodus, Zechariah, Genesis, and Psalms. The later visions should therefore be read with attention to this ongoing scriptural pattern.
